content:
A 5,000 rupee monthly SIP at 12% CAGR produces about 11.6 lakh after 10 years, on a total investment of 6 lakh. That's what every calculator shows. Once you subtract a 1% expense ratio and the 12.5% LTCG tax that has applied since Budget 2024, your actual take-home is around 10.4 to 10.5 lakh. Still a solid gain. Just not the "double your money" figure you sometimes hear.

India's monthly SIP inflows crossed 30,000 crore for three consecutive months through early 2026, according to AMFI. More than 9.7 crore active SIP accounts exist today. At those numbers, the question of what a SIP actually delivers in real terms matters to a lot of people.

Key Takeaways

  • A 5,000/month SIP at 12% CAGR grosses roughly 11.6 lakh in 10 years on 6 lakh invested.
  • Expense ratios and LTCG tax together trim about 1 to 1.2 lakh off that headline number.
  • Equity SIP still beats a recurring deposit by around 2.5 lakh on the same monthly amount and duration.
  • Each year's first 1.25 lakh of long-term gains is tax-free. Stagger redemptions across years to use this.
  • Stopping your SIP during a market downturn is usually the most expensive mistake you can make.

What Does a 5,000 Rupee Monthly SIP Return in 10 Years?

At 12% CAGR, close to the Nifty 50's long-run average, a 5,000 rupee monthly SIP grows to about 11.6 lakh in 10 years. You put in 6 lakh total. The remaining 5.6 lakh is compound growth. That's the gross figure, before the fund's expense ratio and before any tax.

Most calculators stop there. The number is real in the sense that your fund statement will show it. But it isn't what lands in your account when you redeem.

Two things eat into the headline: expense ratios (charged every year, without a line item you'll notice) and LTCG tax (due when you cash out). Neither is catastrophic. Together they're worth understanding before you build a financial plan around a calculator output.

Your actual return can run above or below 12%. The Nifty 50 has delivered roughly 11 to 13% CAGR over rolling 10-year periods, so 12% is a reasonable planning figure for a large-cap equity fund. Small and mid-cap funds have run higher at times and lower in others.

What Actually Cuts Into Your SIP Returns?

Two costs hit every equity SIP. The expense ratio, typically 0.5 to 1.5% per year for active funds and 0.1 to 0.2% for index funds, reduces compounding continuously. Then LTCG tax at 12.5% applies to gains above 1.25 lakh per year when you redeem. Together they trim about 1 to 1.2 lakh off a 10-year 5,000 SIP.

A 1% expense ratio sounds small. Over 10 years it isn't.

If your gross return would be 12%, a 1% expense ratio drops your effective CAGR to roughly 11%. At 11%, the same 5,000 monthly SIP produces about 11 lakh instead of 11.6 lakh. That's 60,000 rupees the fund house keeps, more if you're in a fund with a 1.5% ratio.

Index funds typically charge 0.1 to 0.2%. The extra returns you recieve from keeping costs this low compound meaningfully over a decade. That's one of the stronger arguments for passive investing.

On the tax side: your net gain after expenses is around 5 lakh (11L corpus minus 6L invested). The first 1.25 lakh of long-term gains per year is tax-free under Section 112A. LTCG at 12.5% applies to the remaining roughly 3.75 lakh, working out to about 47,000 rupees in tax. After-tax take-home: around 10.5 lakh.

SIP vs Recurring Deposit vs Savings Account: A Comparison

OptionMonthly10-year corpusAfter-tax take-home
Equity SIP, active fund (11% net CAGR)5,000~11 lakh~10.5 lakh
Equity SIP, index fund (11.8% net CAGR)5,000~11.4 lakh~10.9 lakh
Recurring deposit (7%)5,000~8.7 lakh~8 to 8.2 lakh
Savings account (3.5%)5,000~7.2 lakh~7 lakh

Equity LTCG assumes gains redeemed in one financial year, 12.5% tax above 1.25 lakh exemption. RD and savings interest taxed at 20% income slab. Figures are rounded estimates for planning, not guaranteed returns.

Does a 10-Year Equity SIP Actually Beat Inflation in India?

Yes, but the margin is narrower than the gross numbers suggest. India's inflation has historically run at 5 to 6% per year. A 12% nominal return leaves a real return of roughly 6% annually. That's genuinely inflation-beating. A recurring deposit at 7% barely keeps pace once income tax on interest is applied.

Here's a practical way to think about it. The 10.5 lakh you take home after costs and tax has the same buying power as about 6.1 lakh in today's rupees, assuming 5.5% annual inflation compounded over 10 years.

That sounds modest. But compare it to your alternatives. If you'd kept the same money in a savings account at 3.5%, you'd have roughly 7.2 lakh after 10 years, about 4.2 lakh in today's purchasing power. The equity SIP wins by nearly 2 lakh in real terms.

The stronger comparison is against a recurring deposit. At 7%, an RD produces around 8.7 lakh gross and roughly 8 lakh after income tax on interest. That's meaningfully less than the 10.5 lakh an equity SIP delivers, though the RD carries no market risk at all.

Is a 5,000 Rupee Monthly SIP Enough to Build Real Wealth?

It depends on what you're building toward. At 12% CAGR, a 5,000 monthly SIP reaches roughly 50 lakh in 20 years and about 1.7 crore in 30 years, both gross before tax. That's a reasonable down payment or education corpus. It won't fund a comfortable retirement on its own, especially in a metro.

Most planners in India cite a retirement corpus of at least 3 to 5 crore for a city-based household. A flat 5,000 SIP doesn't reach that in 20 years at any realistic CAGR.

But that's not really the point of starting at 5,000. A step-up SIP, where you increase the monthly amount by 10% each year, nearly doubles the final corpus compared to a flat SIP at the same initial contribution. A flat SIP and a step-up SIP are genuinely different products for planning purposes, and people often conflate them when setting savings goals.

The other thing that is definately worth knowing: stopping your SIP during a market correction is one of the most expensive decisions you can make. The months when markets fall are exactly when rupee-cost averaging works best, because your per-unit price is lowest. Pausing costs you cheap units and the compounding on the recovery that follows.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much will a 5,000 SIP grow in 10 years?

At 12% CAGR, a 5,000 rupee monthly SIP grows to about 11.6 lakh gross in 10 years on 6 lakh invested. After a 1% expense ratio and LTCG tax at 12.5% on gains above 1.25 lakh, the realistic take-home is around 10.4 to 10.5 lakh.

Is SIP return guaranteed?

No. Equity SIP returns are not guaranteed. The 12% figure used in most calculators is based on the Nifty 50's historical CAGR. Actual returns can be higher or lower depending on market cycles, the specific fund, and the period you stay invested.

How does LTCG tax affect SIP returns in 2026?

In 2026, LTCG on equity mutual funds is taxed at 12.5% on annual gains above 1.25 lakh under Section 112A. On a 10-year SIP with roughly 5 lakh in net gains, the tax comes to about 47,000 rupees. Staggering redemptions across two or three financial years reduces this, since the exemption resets each April.

Is SIP better than FD for 10 years?

Generally yes, at a 10-year horizon. An equity SIP at 12% gross delivers roughly 10.5 lakh after tax. A comparable recurring deposit at 7% yields about 8 lakh after income tax on interest. That 2.5 lakh gap is real, though equity SIPs carry market volatility that FDs don't.

What is a step-up SIP and is it worth it?

A step-up SIP raises your monthly contribution by a fixed percentage or amount each year. At 10% annual increase on a 5,000 starting SIP, the 20-year corpus nearly doubles compared to a flat SIP. Worth it for most people whose income is expected to grow over time.

When should I redeem a 10-year SIP?

Start shifting the corpus toward debt or balanced funds 1 to 2 years before you need the money. Redeeming everything at once risks catching a market low. Spreading redemptions across two or three financial years also reduces LTCG tax, since the 1.25 lakh annual exemption resets each April.

The Short Version

A 5,000 rupee monthly SIP gives you roughly 10.5 lakh after expense ratio and LTCG tax, on 6 lakh invested over 10 years. That's real, inflation-beating growth. It won't fund retirement at that contribution level, but it's a solid start. Use an index fund to keep costs low, step up your amount each year, and keep going through market corrections. Those three choices matter more than any fund-selection strategy.
